title: U2’s “Carnaval De Luz” Review: Pitchfork’s Verdict on the Iconic Album’s Legacy
body:
The Irish rock institution U2 has unveiled “Carnaval De Luz,” a sprawling double‑album that marks the band’s most ambitious foray into global pop since the early 2000s, and the reaction from critics is already polarising. In a detailed assessment, Sam Sodomsky praised the record’s audacious sonic palette and its willingness to confront the contradictions of fame, while also noting that the album’s length and eclecticism may alienate listeners who prefer the band’s tighter, anthem‑driven catalog. The review positions “Carnaval De Luz” as both a celebration of U2’s restless curiosity and a reminder of the creative tensions that have defined their career for nearly five decades.

The record opens with “Solar Flare,” a kinetic blend of Afro‑beat percussion, synth‑laden textures, and Bono’s trademark soaring vocals. From there, the album veers through a kaleidoscope of styles—Latin‑inflected ballads, glitch‑pop interludes, and even a brief foray into ambient soundscapes reminiscent of Brian Eno’s early collaborations with the group. Sodomsky highlights the band’s willingness to let producer Brian Eno and co‑producer Daniel Lanois experiment without restraint, resulting in moments that feel both fresh and comfortably familiar. Tracks such as “Mirage of the City” and “Echoes in the Bazaar” showcase The Edge’s signature delay‑heavy guitar work, now filtered through a palette of world‑music scales that give the songs an expansive, borderless quality.

Yet the review does not shy away from the album’s shortcomings. At nearly two hours in length, “Carnaval De Luz” can feel unwieldy, with several interludes that blur the line between artistic experimentation and filler. Sodomsky argues that the sheer breadth of influences sometimes dilutes the emotional core that made earlier U2 records resonate so deeply. The lyrical content, while ambitious, oscillates between poetic abstraction and overt political commentary, leaving listeners to wonder whether the band is speaking from conviction or simply riding the wave of current sociopolitical discourse.

The context of this release is steeped in a long‑standing debate about what constitutes “rock ’n’ roll” in the modern era—a dispute that resurfaced publicly when Bono clashed with veteran music journalist Greg Kot during the height of “Vertigo’s” commercial dominance. Kot, who had framed rock as a raw, guitar‑driven rebellion, argued that U2’s increasingly polished, stadium‑ready sound had strayed from the genre’s roots. Bono, in turn, defended the band’s evolution, insisting that rock is defined more by its spirit of defiance than by any specific instrumentation. “Carnaval De Luz” can be read as a direct response to that argument, embracing a multiplicity of sounds while retaining the band’s signature lyrical urgency, thereby expanding the definition of rock to encompass a global, genre‑blending perspective.

Industry insiders suggest that the album’s release strategy—dropping a double‑LP with a companion visual art book and a series of immersive listening events—signals U2’s intent to reassert themselves as cultural curators rather than merely chart‑topping musicians. The band’s willingness to invest in an elaborate rollout underscores their confidence that the record’s artistic merit will outweigh commercial risk. Early streaming data shows a strong uptick among both longtime fans and younger listeners drawn by the album’s eclectic collaborations with artists from Brazil, Nigeria, and Japan.

Looking ahead, “Carnaval De Luz” may well become a touchstone for legacy acts seeking relevance in an era dominated by genre fluidity and streaming algorithms. Whether the album’s sprawling ambition will translate into sustained chart performance or be relegated to a niche appreciation remains to be seen. What is clear, however, is that U2 has once again sparked conversation about the evolving identity of rock music, proving that even after nearly fifty years, the band can still generate debate, inspire experimentation, and chart a course that challenges both themselves and their audience.
